  "textEditContent": "# Firebase Authentication Setup Guide\n\n*Generated: July 11, 2025*\n\n## 1. What is Firebase Authentication?\n\nFirebase Authentication is a backend-as-a-service (BaaS) that provides ready-to-use UI libraries, SDKs, and backend services to authenticate users to your application. It supports various sign-in methods, including email/password, phone numbers, and federated identity providers like Google, GitHub, and Facebook.\n\nFor DriftBoard, it solves the problem of building a secure, scalable authentication system from scratch, allowing us to focus on core application features.\n\n### How It Works: The Token-Based Flow\n\nThe process is based on JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), which Firebase calls \"ID Tokens.\"\n\n1.  **Client-Side Sign-in**: The user clicks a \"Sign in with Google\" button in the React frontend. The Firebase client-side SDK handles the OAuth flow with Google.\n2.  **Receive ID Token**: After a successful sign-in, Google returns an authentication token to Firebase, which then provides the client app with a Firebase **ID Token (JWT)**. This token contains user information (like a unique &#96;uid&#96;, email, and name) and is cryptographically signed by Firebase.\n3.  **Send Token to Backend**: The React app includes this ID Token in the &#96;Authorization&#96; header of every API request it sends to our Express backend (e.g., &#96;Authorization: Bearer &lt;ID_TOKEN&gt;&#96;).\n4.  **Backend Verification**: The Express backend uses a protected middleware for all relevant routes. This middleware uses the **Firebase Admin SDK** to verify the signature and expiration of the ID Token. This step is secure and ensures the token was issued by Firebase and not tampered with.\n5.  **Access Control**: If the token is valid, the middleware decodes it to get the user's &#96;uid&#96;. It attaches this user information to the Express request object (&#96;req.user&#96;).\n6.  **User-Scoped Data**: The API route handlers then use &#96;req.user.uid&#96; in their Prisma database queries to fetch or modify data that belongs *only* to that specific user.\n\nThis flow ensures that users can only ever access their own boards, lists, and cards.\n\n---\n\n## 2. External Setup (Firebase Console)\n\nBefore writing any code, you need to configure the Firebase project.\n\n1.  **Create Firebase Project**:\n    *   Go to the [Firebase Console](https://console.firebase.google.com/).\n    *   Click \"Add project\" and give it a name (e.g., \"DriftBoard\").\n    *   You can disable Google Analytics for this project if you wish.\n\n2.  **Enable Authentication Providers**:\n    *   In the project dashboard, go to **Build &gt; Authentication**.\n    *   Click \"Get started\".\n    *   In the \"Sign-in method\" tab, enable the providers you want to support (e.g., **Google** and **GitHub**). Follow the on-screen instructions for each.\n\n3.  **Register Your Web App**:\n    *   Go to your Project Settings (click the gear icon next to \"Project Overview\").\n    *   Under \"Your apps\", click the web icon (&#96;&lt;/&gt;&#96;).\n    *   Give your app a nickname (e.g., \"DriftBoard Web\") and click \"Register app\".\n    *   Firebase will provide a &#96;firebaseConfig&#96; object. **Copy this object.** You will need it for your frontend application.\n\n4.  **Generate Backend Service Account Credentials**:\n    *   In your Project Settings, go to the **Service accounts** tab.\n    *   Click the \"Generate new private key\" button.\n    *   This will download a JSON file. **Rename this file to &#96;firebase-service-account.json&#96;** and place it in a secure location in your backend directory (ensure it's added to &#96;.gitignore&#96;). This file gives your backend server admin access to your Firebase project.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Internal Setup (Codebase)\n\n### Frontend (React + Vite)\n\n1.  **Install Firebase SDK**:\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;bash\n    npm install firebase\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n2.  **Initialize Firebase**:\n    *   Create a new file: &#96;src/frontend/src/firebase.ts&#96;.\n    *   Add the &#96;firebaseConfig&#96; object you copied earlier.\n\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;typescript\n    // src/frontend/src/firebase.ts\n    import { initializeApp } from 'firebase/app';\n    import { getAuth } from 'firebase/auth';\n\n    const firebaseConfig = {\n      apiKey: \"...\",\n      authDomain: \"...\",\n      projectId: \"...\",\n      storageBucket: \"...\",\n      messagingSenderId: \"...\",\n      appId: \"...\"\n    };\n\n    const app = initializeApp(firebaseConfig);\n    export const auth = getAuth(app);\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n3.  **Integrate with RTK Query**:\n    *   Update your RTK Query API definition to automatically add the auth token to every request.\n\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;typescript\n    // src/frontend/src/store/api.ts (or similar)\n    import { fetchBaseQuery } from '@reduxjs/toolkit/query/react';\n    import { auth } from '../firebase'; // Adjust path\n\n    export const baseQuery = fetchBaseQuery({\n      baseUrl: '/api',\n      prepareHeaders: async (headers) =&gt; {\n        const user = auth.currentUser;\n        if (user) {\n          const token = await user.getIdToken();\n          headers.set('Authorization', &#96;Bearer ${token}&#96;);\n        }\n        return headers;\n      },\n    });\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n4.  **Create Auth Components**:\n    *   Implement a &#96;LoginPage.tsx&#96; with \"Sign in\" buttons.\n    *   Create an &#96;AuthGate&#96; or &#96;ProtectedRoute&#96; component that uses &#96;onAuthStateChanged&#96; from the Firebase SDK to listen to the user's auth state and redirect them appropriately.\n\n### Backend (Express.js)\n\n1.  **Install Firebase Admin SDK**:\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;bash\n    # In your src/backend directory\n    npm install firebase-admin\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n2.  **Initialize Admin SDK**:\n    *   Update your main server file or a dedicated config file.\n\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;typescript\n    // src/backend/server.ts (or a new src/backend/firebase.ts)\n    import * as admin from 'firebase-admin';\n\n    // IMPORTANT: Place the downloaded JSON file in your backend directory\n    const serviceAccount = require('./firebase-service-account.json'); // Adjust path\n\n    admin.initializeApp({\n      credential: admin.credential.cert(serviceAccount),\n    });\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n3.  **Create Authentication Middleware**:\n    *   This middleware will protect your API routes.\n\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;typescript\n    // src/backend/middleware/authMiddleware.ts\n    import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';\n    import * as admin from 'firebase-admin';\n\n    export const authMiddleware = async (req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) =&gt; {\n      const token = req.headers.authorization?.split('Bearer ')[1];\n\n      if (!token) {\n        return res.status(401).send({ error: 'Unauthorized: No token provided' });\n      }\n\n      try {\n        const decodedToken = await admin.auth().verifyIdToken(token);\n        // You can augment the Request type to include &#96;user&#96;\n        (req as any).user = decodedToken;\n        next();\n      } catch (error) {\n        console.error('Error verifying auth token:', error);\n        return res.status(403).send({ error: 'Forbidden: Invalid token' });\n      }\n    };\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n4.  **Protect Routes**:\n    *   Apply the middleware to all routes that require authentication.\n\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;typescript\n    // src/backend/routes/boards.ts\n    import { Router } from 'express';\n    import { authMiddleware } from '../middleware/authMiddleware';\n\n    const router = Router();\n    router.use(authMiddleware); // Protect all board routes\n\n    // All handlers below this line will have access to req.user\n    router.get('/', getBoardsHandler);\n    &#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n---\n\n## 4. VS Code Extensions for Firebase\n\nWhile there isn't a dedicated MCP tool specifically for Firebase, you can significantly improve your workflow in VS Code with the right extensions.\n\n-   **Firebase** (by Google, ID: &#96;google.firebase-vscode&#96;): This is the official extension. # Phase 2 Implementation Plan: Enhanced Functionality & Technical Excellence
*Generated: July 10, 2025*
## 1. Overview
Following the successful completion of Phase 1, Phase 2 focuses on delivering high-impact user features, addressing key technical debt, and preparing the application for multi-user, production-ready deployment. This plan breaks down the work into logical, sequential sub-phases to ensure steady progress and maintain architectural integrity.
## 2. Phase 2 Sub-Phases
Phase 2 is divided into four main sub-phases, each with a clear focus:
- **Phase 2a: Core Interactions & Testing Foundation** - **COMPLETED**
- **Phase 2b: Authentication & User Scope** - **IN PROGRESS**
- **Phase 2c: Rich Content & Enhanced Metadata** - Add features that enrich the card and board data.
- **Phase 2d: Quality, Performance & Production Readiness** - Focus on hardening the application, optimizing performance, and finalizing production setup.
---
## 3. Phase 2a: Core Interactions & Testing Foundation
**Status: COMPLETED**
**Focus**: Implement the highest-priority user feature—drag-and-drop—and build the initial testing infrastructure to support it.
### 3.1. Feature: Drag & Drop (`@dnd-kit`)
- **Problem**: Users cannot reorder cards and lists visually, which is a core Kanban experience.
- **Technical Approach**:
    - Integrate `@dnd-kit` for its robust, accessible, and framework-agnostic drag-and-drop capabilities.
    - Implement `DndContext` at the board level.
    - Create sortable contexts for both lists and cards within lists.
    - Develop new API endpoints (`/cards/:id/move`, `/lists/:id/move`) to handle position updates.
    - Use optimistic UI updates in RTK Query to provide immediate visual feedback during drag operations.
- **Implementation Steps**:
    1. ✅ Install `@dnd-kit/core`, `@dnd-kit/sortable`.
    2. ✅ Create a `DragDropProvider` component to encapsulate the DnD context.
    3. ✅ Make `List` and `Card` components draggable using `useDraggable` and `useSortable`.
    4. ✅ Implement `handleDragEnd` logic to dispatch API calls for reordering.
    5. ✅ Update Prisma schema (`position` fields to `Float`) and services to use decimal-based positioning for efficient reordering.
### 3.2. Technical Debt: E2E & Component Tests
- **Problem**: No automated tests exist for frontend user interactions.
- **Technical Approach**:
    - Use Playwright to create E2E tests for the new drag-and-drop functionality.
    - Use Vitest and React Testing Library to create unit/integration tests for the key DnD components.
- **Implementation Steps**:
    1. ✅ Write a Playwright test spec (`dnd.spec.ts`) that simulates dragging a card between lists and verifies the final state.
    2. ✅ Write component tests for `KanbanCard` and `List` to ensure they respond correctly to drag events.
---
## 4. Phase 2b: Authentication & User Scope
**Status: IN PROGRESS**
**Focus**: Transition from a single-user application to a multi-user, secure platform using Firebase Authentication.
### 4.1. Feature: Firebase Authentication
- **Problem**: The application lacks user accounts, security, and data isolation.
- **Technical Approach**:
    - Integrate Firebase Auth for Google and GitHub sign-in.
    - Update the Prisma schema to associate all data (boards, lists, cards) with a `userId`.
    - Create backend middleware to validate Firebase JWTs and attach the user to the request object.
    - Refactor all API service logic to be user-aware, ensuring users can only access their own data.
- **Implementation Steps**:
    1. 🔘 Set up a new Firebase project and configure Auth.
    2. 🔘 Add `User` model to `schema.prisma` and link it to the `Board` model.
    3. 🔘 Create `authMiddleware` in the backend to protect all routes.
    4. 🔘 Update all database queries to include a `where: { userId: ... }` clause.
    5. 🔘 Implement frontend login page, auth state management (in a Redux slice), and routing guards.
---
## 5. Phase 2c: Rich Content & Enhanced Metadata
**Focus**: Enhance the value of cards by adding more detailed information and tracking history.
### 5.1. Feature: Rich Content & Metadata
- **Problem**: Cards are limited to a title and description. Users need labels, due dates, and rich text formatting.
- **Technical Approach**:
    - **Rich Editing**: Integrate a lightweight Markdown library (e.g., `react-markdown`) to render card descriptions.
    - **Labels & Due Dates**:
        - Extend the `Card` model in `schema.prisma` to include `dueDate` (DateTime) and a many-to-many relation to a new `Label` model.
        - Create new API endpoints for managing labels (`/api/labels`).
        - Update the `CardModal` component to include UI for setting a due date and assigning labels.
- **Implementation Steps**:
    1. Add `Label` and `Activity` models to the Prisma schema and update the `Card` model.
    2. Build the backend API for CRUD operations on labels.
    3. Update the frontend `Card` component and `CardModal` to display and edit this new metadata.
    4. Implement `react-markdown` in the `CardModal` for the description field.
### 5.2. Feature: Activity History
- **Problem**: There is no audit trail for changes made to cards.
- **Technical Approach**:
    - Create an `Activity` model in Prisma linked to cards.
    - In the backend, create a generic `createActivity` service that is called from other services (e.g., after updating a card's title, moving a card).
    - Display the activity feed within the `CardModal`.
- **Implementation Steps**:
    1. Add the `Activity` model to `schema.prisma`.
    2. Implement the backend logic to log activities for all relevant card and list mutations.
    3. Add an "Activity" section to the `CardModal` component that fetches and displays the history.
---
## 6. Phase 2d: Quality, Performance & Production Readiness
**Focus**: Address remaining technical debt, optimize for large datasets, and finalize the production environment.
### 6.1. Technical Debt: Testing, Performance & Errors
- **Problem**: The application needs comprehensive testing, performance tuning, and more robust error handling.
- **Technical Approach**:
    - **Testing**: Achieve 80%+ component test coverage. Write E2E tests for all critical user flows (auth, board creation, etc.).
    - **Performance**:
        - Implement virtualization (`react-virtual`) for lists and cards to handle boards with thousands of items.
        - Analyze and optimize expensive database queries.
    - **Error Boundaries**: Wrap key feature areas in React Error Boundaries to prevent UI crashes.
- **Implementation Steps**:
    1. Write comprehensive component tests for all pages and business components.
    2. Implement `useVirtual` hook for rendering long lists of cards.
    3. Wrap the main `BoardDetailPage` in an `ErrorBoundary` component.
### 6.2. Feature: Search
- **Problem**: Users cannot find cards across the entire application.
- **Technical Approach**:
    - Implement a new backend endpoint (`/api/search?q=...`) that performs a full-text search across card titles and descriptions for the authenticated user.
    - Add a global search bar to the application layout.
- **Implementation Steps**:
    1. Create the search endpoint in the backend.
    2. Add a search input to the frontend `Header` component.
    3. Display search results in a dropdown or a dedicated search results page.
### 6.3. Technical Debt: Production Docker & CI/CD
- **Problem**: The Docker setup is not optimized for production.
- **Technical Approach**:
    - Refine the `Dockerfile` to use multi-stage builds for smaller, more secure production images.
    - Ensure all secrets and environment variables are handled correctly.
    - Set up a basic CI/CD pipeline using GitHub Actions to build, test, and (optionally) deploy the application.

- **Implementation Steps**:

    1. Optimize the `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` for a production environment.

    2. Create a GitHub Actions workflow file to run tests on every push.


```

Excellent. You've completed the first steps for the frontend.

The next step, according to our plan, is to update the database schema to support multiple users. This involves ensuring each board is associated with a user.

I've updated  to add the relationship between the `User` and `Board` models. Specifically, I've added a `userId` field to the `Board` model and established a formal relation. This ensures that every board must belong to a user, and if a user is ever deleted, all of their associated boards will be removed automatically (`onDelete: Cascade`).

Now that the schema is updated, we need to apply these changes to your database by running a migration. I'll do that now. ```prisma
// This is your Prisma schema file,
// learn more about it in the docs: https://pris.ly/d/prisma-schema
generator client {
  provider = "prisma-client-js"
  output   = "../src/shared/generated/prisma"
}
datasource db {
  provider = "sqlite"
  url      = env("DATABASE_URL")
}
model User {
  id        String   @id // This will be the Firebase UID
  email     String   @unique
  name      String?
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
  updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt
  boards    Board[]
  @@map("users")
}
model Board {
  id          String    @id @default(cuid())
  name        String
  description String?
  createdAt   DateTime  @default(now())
  updatedAt   DateTime  @updatedAt
  archivedAt  DateTime?
  lists List[]
  user   User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  userId String
  @@index([userId])
  @@map("boards")
}
model List {
  id        String   @id @default(cuid())
  name      String
  boardId   String
  position  Float
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
  updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt
  board     Board    @relation(fields: [boardId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  cards     Card[]
  @@index([boardId])
  @@map("lists")
}
model Card {
  id          String     @id @default(cuid())
  title       String
  description String?
  listId      String
  position    Float
  dueDate     DateTime?
  createdAt   DateTime   @default(now())
  updatedAt   DateTime   @updatedAt
  list        List       @relation(fields: [listId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  labels      Label[]
  activities  Activity[]
  @@index([listId])
  @@map("cards")
}
model Label {
  id     String @id @default(cuid())
  name   String
  color  String
  cardId String
  card   Card   @relation(fields: [cardId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  @@index([cardId])
  @@map("labels")
}
model Activity {
  id        String   @id @default(cuid())
  type      String   // 'comment', 'moved', 'edited', 'created', 'archived'
  content   String?
  cardId    String
  userId    String
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
  card      Card     @relation(fields: [cardId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  @@index([cardId])
  @@index([userId])
  @@map("activities")
}

I've also replaced the placeholder authentication middleware with a real one that uses the Firebase Admin SDK to verify ID tokens. I noticed the previous edit introduced a few TypeScript errors, so I've corrected them by:

Here are the changes to : ```typescript
import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import * as admin from 'firebase-admin';
import { AppError } from './errorHandler.js';
// Extend Request type to include user
declare global {
  namespace Express {
    interface Request {
      user?: admin.auth.DecodedIdToken;
    }
  }
}
/**
 * Middleware to verify Firebase ID token.
 */
export const authMiddleware = async (
  req: Request,
  res: Response,
  next: NextFunction,
): Promise<void> => {

import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import * as admin from 'firebase-admin';
import { AppError } from './errorHandler.js';
// Extend Request type to include user
declare global {
  namespace Express {
    interface Request {
      user?: admin.auth.DecodedIdToken;
    }
  }
}
/**
 * Middleware to verify Firebase ID token.
 */
export const authMiddleware = async (
  req: Request,
  _res: Response,
  next: NextFunction,
): Promise<void> => {
  // Bypass auth for test environment for easier API testing
  if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'test') {
    req.user = {
      uid: 'test-user-id',
      email: 'test@example.com',
      name: 'Test User',
    } as unknown as admin.auth.DecodedIdToken; // Cast to bypass strict type checking for mock
    return next();
  }
  const authHeader = req.headers.authorization;
  if (!authHeader || !authHeader.startsWith('Bearer ')) {
    return next(new AppError('Unauthorized: No token provided or invalid format', 401, 'NO_TOKEN'));
  }
  const idToken = authHeader.split('Bearer ')[1];
  if (!idToken) {
    return next(new AppError('Unauthorized: Token is missing', 401, 'NO_TOKEN'));
  }
  try {
    const decodedToken = await admin.auth().verifyIdToken(idToken);
    req.user = decodedToken;
    next();
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error verifying Firebase ID token:', error);

    next(new AppError('Forbidden: Invalid or expired token', 403, 'INVALID_TOKEN'));

  }

};

export interface User {

  userId: string;

  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
  lists?: List[];

  id: string;

  boardId: string;
  position: number;
  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
  cards?: Card[];
}

  description: string | null;
  listId: string;
  position: number;

  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
  labels?: Label[];
  activities?: Activity[];
}

  name: string;

}

  id: string;

  userId: string;

}

  position?: number;

  description?: string;

    total: number;

}

    }
    await prisma.board.delete({
      where: { id: boardId },
    });
    const response: ApiResponse = {

/**
 * Create a list in a board
 * POST /api/boards/:id/lists

router.post('/:id/lists', async (req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {
  try {
    const userId = req.user?.uid;
    const boardId = req.params.id;
    if (!userId) {
      throw new AppError('User not authenticated', 401, 'NOT_AUTHENTICATED');
    }
    if (!boardId) {
      throw new AppError('Board ID is required', 400, 'INVALID_INPUT');
    }
    const { name, position }: { name: string; position?: number } = req.body;
    if (!name || name.trim().length === 0) {
      throw new AppError('List name is required', 400, 'MISSING_LIST_NAME');
    }
    // Verify board exists and belongs to user
    const board = await prisma.board.findFirst({
      where: { 
        id: boardId,
        userId,
      },
    });
    if (!board) {
      throw new AppError('Board not found', 404, 'BOARD_NOT_FOUND');
    }
    // Calculate position if not provided
    let listPosition = position;
    if (listPosition === undefined) {
      const maxPosition = await prisma.list.aggregate({
        where: { boardId },
        _max: { position: true },
      });
      listPosition = (maxPosition._max?.position ?? -1) + 1;
    } else {
      // If position is specified, shift existing lists
      await prisma.list.updateMany({
        where: {
          boardId,
          position: {
            gte: listPosition,
          },
        },
        data: {
          position: {
            increment: 1,
          },
        },
      });
    }
    const list = await prisma.list.create({
      data: {
        name: name.trim(),
        boardId,
        position: listPosition,
      },
      include: {
        cards: {
          orderBy: { position: 'asc' },
          include: {
            labels: true,
          },
        },
      },
    });
    const response: ApiResponse = {
      success: true,
      data: list,
      message: 'List created successfully',
    };
    res.status(201).json(response);
  } catch (error) {
    next(error);
  }
});
export { router as boardsRouter };

import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'vitest';
import supertest from 'supertest';
import app from '../../src/backend/server';
import { prisma } from '../../src/backend/services/database';
const request = supertest(app);
// Mock the firebase-admin module
vi.mock('firebase-admin', () => ({
  initializeApp: vi.fn(),
  auth: () => ({
    verifyIdToken: vi.fn().mockImplementation(async (token) => {
      if (token === 'valid-token') {
        return { uid: 'test-user-id', email: 'test@example.com' };
      }
      throw new Error('Invalid token');
    }),
  }),
}));
describe('Authentication Middleware', () => {
  const testUserId = 'test-user-id';
  beforeAll(async () => {
    // Create a test user and a board for that user
    await prisma.user.create({
      data: {
        id: testUserId,
        email: 'test@example.com',
        name: 'Test User',
        boards: {
          create: {
            name: 'Test Board',
          },
        },
      },
    });
  });
  afterAll(async () => {
    // Clean up the database
    await prisma.board.deleteMany({ where: { userId: testUserId } });
    await prisma.user.delete({ where: { id: testUserId } });
    await prisma.$disconnect();
  });
  it('should return 401 if no Authorization header is provided', async () => {
    const response = await request.get('/api/boards');
    expect(response.status).toBe(401);
    expect(response.body.error).toContain('No token provided');
  });
  it('should return 403 if the token is invalid', async () => {
    const response = await request
      .get('/api/boards')
      .set('Authorization', 'Bearer invalid-token');
    expect(response.status).toBe(403);
    expect(response.body.error).toContain('Invalid or expired token');
  });
  it('should return 200 and data if the token is valid', async () => {
    const response = await request
      .get('/api/boards')
      .set('Authorization', 'Bearer valid-token');
    
    expect(response.status).toBe(200);
    expect(response.body.success).toBe(true);
    expect(response.body.data).toBeInstanceOf(Array);
    expect(response.body.data.length).toBe(1);
    expect(response.body.data[0].name).toBe('Test Board');
  });
  it('should prevent a user from accessing another user\'s data', async () => {
    // This test relies on the mock always returning 'test-user-id' as the uid.
    // We try to access a board that doesn't belong to this user.
    const otherUserBoard = await prisma.board.create({
        data: {
            name: 'Other User Board',
            user: {
                create: {
                    id: 'other-user-id',
                    email: 'other@example.com',
                }
            }
        }
    });
    const response = await request
      .get(`/api/boards/${otherUserBoard.id}`)
      .set('Authorization', 'Bearer valid-token');
    // The user is authenticated, but the board should not be found for them.
    expect(response.status).toBe(404);
    expect(response.body.error).toContain('Board not found');
    // Cleanup
    await prisma.board.delete({ where: { id: otherUserBoard.id }});
    await prisma.user.delete({ where: { id: 'other-user-id' }});
  });
});

        .delete(`/api/boards/${board1.id}`)

        .set('Authorization', 'Bearer valid-token-user-1');

      expect(dbBoard).toBeNull();

    });

  describe('User creation on first login', () => {

      const newUserUid = 'new-user-id';

      const newUserEmail = 'new@example.com';



      // Extend the mock to handle the new user token

      const { auth } = await import('firebase-admin');

      (auth().verifyIdToken as any).mockImplementation(async (token: string) => {

        if (token === 'valid-token-user-1') return { uid: 'user-1-id', email: 'user1@test.com' };

        if (token === 'valid-token-user-2') return { uid: 'user-2-id', email: 'user2@test.com' };

        if (token === newUserToken) return { uid: newUserUid, email: newUserEmail };

        throw new Error('Invalid token');

      });



      // Make sure user does not exist

      let dbUser = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id: newUserUid } });

      expect(dbUser).toBeNull();



      // Make first request

      const response = await request

        .get('/api/boards')

        .set('Authorization', `Bearer ${newUserToken}`);



      expect(response.status).toBe(200);

      expect(response.body.data).toEqual([]);



      // Verify user was created

      dbUser = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id: newUserUid } });

      expect(dbUser).not.toBeNull();

      expect(dbUser?.email).toBe(newUserEmail);

    });

  });

});

import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import * as admin from 'firebase-admin';
import { AppError } from './errorHandler.js';
import prisma from '../services/database.js';
// Extend Request type to include user
declare global {
  namespace Express {
    interface Request {
      user?: admin.auth.DecodedIdToken & { id: string }; // Ensure id is available
    }
  }
}
/**
 * Middleware to verify Firebase ID token and handle user creation.
 */
export const authMiddleware = async (
  req: Request,
  _res: Response,
  next: NextFunction,
): Promise<void> => {
  // In test environment, mock user from a special header
  if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'test') {
    const testUserUid = req.headers['x-test-user-uid'] as string;
    if (testUserUid) {
      // This mock allows us to test authenticated routes
      req.user = {
        uid: testUserUid,
        email: `${testUserUid}@example.com`,
        name: 'Test User',
        id: testUserUid, // For consistency
      } as admin.auth.DecodedIdToken & { id: string };
      return next();
    }
    // If no header, proceed as unauthenticated to test protected routes
  }
  const authHeader = req.headers.authorization;
  if (!authHeader || !authHeader.startsWith('Bearer ')) {
    return next(new AppError('Unauthorized: No token provided or invalid format', 401, 'NO_TOKEN'));
  }
  const idToken = authHeader.split('Bearer ')[1];
  if (!idToken) {
    return next(new AppError('Unauthorized: Token is missing', 401, 'NO_TOKEN'));
  }
  try {
    const decodedToken = await admin.auth().verifyIdToken(idToken);



    // Check if user exists in our DB, if not, create them

    let user = await prisma.user.findUnique({

      where: { id: decodedToken.uid },

    });



    if (!user) {

      user = await prisma.user.create({

        data: {

          id: decodedToken.uid,

          email: decodedToken.email || '', // email is optional on firebase token

          name: decodedToken.name,

        },

      });

      console.log(`New user created: ${user.id} - ${user.email}`);

    }



    req.user = { ...decodedToken, id: user.id }; // Attach user to request

    next();

  } catch (error) {

    console.error('Error verifying Firebase ID token:', error);

    next(new AppError('Forbidden: Invalid or expired token', 403, 'INVALID_TOKEN'));

  }

};

The tests are failing primarily due to the new authentication logic not being correctly handled in the integration tests. Here's the breakdown of issues and my plan to resolve them:

1.  **Foreign Key Violation**: The  calls are failing because they don't include the new mandatory . This is happening in the setup phase of  and .
2.  **Incorrect Test Assertions**: Many tests in  and  are failing because:
    *   They don't simulate an authenticated user correctly under the new  logic, which now requires a `x-test-user-uid` header.
    *   They assert the entire  is an array, but the API now wraps data in an  object (e.g., `{ success: true, data: [...] }`).
    *   They expect 401/403 errors that the test-mode middleware was previously bypassing.
3.  **Missing User Scoping**: The database queries in the `boards.ts`, , and  route handlers do not consistently use  in their  clauses, leading to "Board not found" or "Record to update not found" errors when a query fails to find a record matching both the item ID *and* the user ID.
4.  **User Auto-Creation Failure**: The test for creating a user on their first login is failing because the original middleware didn't have this logic. The new middleware I just wrote should fix this, but the test needs to be adapted to use the new header-based authentication.

I will now systematically fix the backend routes and the corresponding integration tests. I'll start with the `boards.ts` routes and  and . ```typescript
import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import * as admin from 'firebase-admin';
import { AppError } from './errorHandler.js';
import { prisma } from '../services/database.js';
// Extend Request type to include user
declare global {
  namespace Express {
    interface Request {
      user?: admin.auth.DecodedIdToken & { id: string }; // Ensure id is available
    }
  }
}
/**
 * Middleware to verify Firebase ID token and handle user creation.
 */
export const authMiddleware = async (
  req: Request,
  _res: Response,
  next: NextFunction,
): Promise<void> => {
  // In test environment, mock user from a special header
  if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'test') {
    const testUserUid = req.headers['x-test-user-uid'] as string;
    if (testUserUid) {
      // This mock allows us to test authenticated routes
      req.user = {
        uid: testUserUid,
        email: `${testUserUid}@example.com`,
        name: 'Test User',
        id: testUserUid, // For consistency
      } as unknown as admin.auth.DecodedIdToken & { id: string };
      return next();
    }
    // If no header, proceed as unauthenticated to test protected routes
  }
  const authHeader = req.headers.authorization;
  if (!authHeader || !authHeader.startsWith('Bearer ')) {
    return next(new AppError('Unauthorized: No token provided or invalid format', 401, 'NO_TOKEN'));
  }
  const idToken = authHeader.split('Bearer ')[1];
  if (!idToken) {
    return next(new AppError('Unauthorized: Token is missing', 401, 'NO_TOKEN'));
  }
  try {
    const decodedToken = await admin.auth().verifyIdToken(idToken);
    // Check if user exists in our DB, if not, create them
    let user = await prisma.user.findUnique({
      where: { id: decodedToken.uid },
    });
    if (!user) {
      user = await prisma.user.create({
        data: {
          id: decodedToken.uid,
          email: decodedToken.email || '', // email is optional on firebase token
          name: decodedToken.name,
        },
      });
      console.log(`New user created: ${user.id} - ${user.email}`);
    }
    req.user = { ...decodedToken, id: user.id }; // Attach user to request
    next();
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error verifying Firebase ID token:', error);
    next(new AppError('Forbidden: Invalid or expired token', 403, 'INVALID_TOKEN'));
  }
};
```

    res.json(response);

router.put('/:id', async (req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {

    const boardId = req.params.id;
    const { name, description } = req.body as UpdateBoardDto;
    if (!userId) {

    }
    // Verify board exists and belongs to user
    const existingBoard = await prisma.board.findUnique({
      where: {

      },
    });
    if (!existingBoard || existingBoard.userId !== userId) {
      throw new AppError('Board not found or access denied', 404, 'BOARD_NOT_FOUND');
    }
    await prisma.board.delete({
      where: { id: boardId },
    });
    const response: ApiResponse = {
      success: true,
      message: 'Board deleted successfully',
    };
    res.status(204).send();
  } catch (error) {
    next(error);
  }
});

 * POST /api/boards/:id/lists
 */
router.post('/:id/lists', async (req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {
  try {
    const userId = req.user?.uid;
    const boardId = req.params.id;
    if (!userId) {
      throw new AppError('User not authenticated', 401, 'NOT_AUTHENTICATED');
    }
    if (!boardId) {
      throw new AppError('Board ID is required', 400, 'INVALID_INPUT');
    }
    const { name, position }: { name: string; position?: number } = req.body;
    if (!name || name.trim().length === 0) {
      throw new AppError('List name is required', 400, 'MISSING_LIST_NAME');
    }
    // Verify board exists and belongs to user
    const board = await prisma.board.findFirst({
      where: { 
        id: boardId,
        userId,
      },
    });
    if (!board) {
      throw new AppError('Board not found', 404, 'BOARD_NOT_FOUND');
    }
    // Calculate position if not provided
    let listPosition = position;
    if (listPosition === undefined) {
      const maxPosition = await prisma.list.aggregate({
        where: { boardId },
        _max: { position: true },
      });
      listPosition = (maxPosition._max?.position ?? -1) + 1;
    } else {
      // If position is specified, shift existing lists
      await prisma.list.updateMany({
        where: {
          boardId,
          position: {
            gte: listPosition,
          },
        },
        data: {
          position: {
            increment: 1,
          },
        },
      });
    }
    const list = await prisma.list.create({
      data: {
        name: name.trim(),
        boardId,
        position: listPosition,
      },
      include: {
        cards: {
          orderBy: { position: 'asc' },
          include: {
            labels: true,
          },
        },
      },
    });
    const response: ApiResponse = {
      success: true,
      data: list,
      message: 'List created successfully',
    };

    res.status(201).json(response);

  } catch (error) {

    next(error);

  }

});



export { router as boardsRouter };

import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import supertest from 'supertest';
import app from '../../src/backend/server';
import { prisma } from '../../src/backend/services/database';
// Mock Firebase Admin SDK
vi.mock('firebase-admin', () => ({
  auth: () => ({
    verifyIdToken: vi.fn().mockImplementation(async (token) => {

      // Verify user was created

      expect(dbUser).not.toBeNull();
      expect(dbUser?.email).toBe(`${newUserUid}@example.com`);
    });
  });
});

import dotenv from 'dotenv';
import { errorHandler } from './middleware/errorHandler.js';
import { requestLogger } from './middleware/requestLogger.js';
import { authMiddleware } from './middleware/authMiddleware.js';
import { healthRouter } from './routes/health.js';
import { authRouter } from './routes/auth.js';
import { boardsRouter } from './routes/boards.js';
import { listsRouter } from './routes/lists.js';
import { cardsRouter } from './routes/cards.js';
// Load environment variables
dotenv.config();
const app = express();
const NODE_ENV = process.env.NODE_ENV || 'development';
const PORT =
  process.env.PORT ||
  (NODE_ENV === 'production' ? 8000 : NODE_ENV === 'test' ? 8002 : 8001);
// Security middleware
app.use(helmet({
  contentSecurityPolicy: {
    directives: {
      defaultSrc: ["'self'"],
      styleSrc: ["'self'", "'unsafe-inline'"],
      scriptSrc: ["'self'"],
      imgSrc: ["'self'", "data:", "https:"],
      connectSrc: ["'self'", "https://identitytoolkit.googleapis.com", "https://securetoken.googleapis.com"],
    },
  },
}));
// CORS configuration

  origin: process.env.CORS_ORIGINS?.split(',') || ['http://localhost:3000', 'http://localhost:5173'],
  credentials: true,
  optionsSuccessStatus: 200,
};
app.use(cors(corsOptions));
// Compression middleware
app.use(compression());
// Body parsing middleware
app.use(express.json({ limit: '10mb' }));
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: true, limit: '10mb' }));
// Request logging
app.use(requestLogger);
// Health check (no auth required)
app.use('/api/health', healthRouter);
// Auth routes (no auth required for login/register)
app.use('/api/auth', authRouter);
// Protected API routes
app.use('/api/boards', authMiddleware, boardsRouter);
app.use('/api/lists', authMiddleware, listsRouter);
app.use('/api/cards', authMiddleware, cardsRouter);
// Error handling middleware (must be last)
app.use(errorHandler);
// Graceful shutdown handling
process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  console.log('🛑 SIGTERM received, shutting down gracefully...');
  process.exit(0);
});
process.on('SIGINT', () => {
  console.log('🛑 SIGINT received, shutting down gracefully...');
  process.exit(0);
});
// Only start server if this file is run directly (not imported)

  app.listen(PORT, () => {
    console.log(`🚀 DriftBoard server running on port ${PORT}`);
    console.log(`📱 Environment: ${NODE_ENV}`);
    console.log(`🔗 API Base URL: http://localhost:${PORT}/api`);
    
    if (NODE_ENV === 'production') {
      console.log(`🌐 Frontend served at: http://localhost:${PORT}`);
    }
  });
}

export default app;

6.  **Protected Routes ():** A component that wraps private routes, redirecting unauthenticated users to the login page.
7.  **App Routing ():**
    *   Reworked the main  component to handle application-wide routing.
    *   It now listens for changes in Firebase authentication state and updates the Redux store accordingly.
    *   It uses the  component to secure the main application pages, making the login page the only publicly accessible route.

I encountered a small error in  regarding the  component expecting `children`. I will fix that now by reading the  file and adjusting the  file accordingly. ```tsx
import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom';
import { useDispatch } from 'react-redux';
import { onAuthStateChanged } from 'firebase/auth';
import { AppLayout } from '@/components/layout/AppLayout';
import { ProtectedRoute } from './components/ProtectedRoute';
import { BoardsPage } from './pages/BoardsPage';
import { BoardDetailPage } from './pages/BoardDetailPage';
import { LoginPage } from './pages/LoginPage';
import { auth } from './firebase';
import { setUser, setLoading } from './store/authSlice';
import './App.css';
function App() {
  const dispatch = useDispatch();
  useEffect(() => {
    const unsubscribe = onAuthStateChanged(auth, async (user) => {
      if (user) {

        const idToken = await user.getIdToken();

        dispatch(setUser({

          uid: user.uid,

          email: user.email,

          displayName: user.displayName,

          idToken,

        }));

      } else {

        dispatch(setUser(null));

      }

      dispatch(setLoading(false));

    });



    return () => unsubscribe();

  }, [dispatch]);



  return (

    <Routes>

      <Route path="/login" element={<LoginPage />} />

      <Route element={<ProtectedRoute />}>

        <Route element={<AppLayout />}>

          <Route path="/" element={<BoardsPage />} />

          <Route path="/boards" element={<BoardsPage />} />

          <Route path="/boards/:id" element={<BoardDetailPage />} />

        </Route>

      </Route>

    </Routes>

  );

}



export default App;


```

*   **Application Routing**: Overhauled  to:
    *   Listen for real-time authentication state changes from Firebase.

    *   Protect the main application routes using the .
*   **Layout Update**: Modified  to use `react-router-dom`'s `<Outlet />` for nested routing, making it compatible with the new protected route structure.

With these changes, the frontend application now supports a full authentication flow. Users will be required to log in to access the Kanban boards, and all subsequent interactions with the backend API will be authenticated.```typescript
import { createApi, fetchBaseQuery } from '@reduxjs/toolkit/query/react';
import { RootState } from '../store';
import { 
  BoardWithDetails, 
  CreateBoardDto, 
  UpdateBoardDto, 
  List,
  CreateListDto,
  UpdateListDto,
  MoveListDto,
  Card,
  CreateCardDto,
  UpdateCardDto,
  MoveCardDto,
  ApiResponse 
} from '@/shared/types';
export const api = createApi({
  reducerPath: 'api',
  baseQuery: fetchBaseQuery({
    baseUrl: '/api',
    prepareHeaders: (headers, { getState }) => {
      const token = (getState() as RootState).auth.user?.idToken;
      if (token) {
        headers.set('authorization', `Bearer ${token}`);
      }
      return headers;
    },
  }),
  tagTypes: ['Board', 'List', 'Card'],
  endpoints: (builder) => ({
    // ===== BOARDS =====
    getBoards: builder.query<BoardWithDetails[], void>({
      query: () => '/boards',
      transformResponse: (response: ApiResponse<BoardWithDetails[]>) => response.data || [],
      providesTags: ['Board'],
    }),
    getBoardById: builder.query<BoardWithDetails, string>({
      query: (id) => `/boards/${id}`,
      transformResponse: (response: ApiResponse<BoardWithDetails>) => response.data!,
      providesTags: (_result, _error, id) => [{ type: 'Board', id }],
    }),
    createBoard: builder.mutation<BoardWithDetails, CreateBoardDto>({
      query: (board) => ({
        url: '/boards',
        method: 'POST',
        body: board,
      }),
      transformResponse: (response: ApiResponse<BoardWithDetails>) => response.data!,
      invalidatesTags: ['Board'],
    }),
    updateBoard: builder.mutation<BoardWithDetails, { id: string; updates: UpdateBoardDto }>({
      query: ({ id, updates }) => ({
        url: `/boards/${id}`,
        method: 'PUT',
        body: updates,
      }),
      transformResponse: (response: ApiResponse<BoardWithDetails>) => response.data!,
      invalidatesTags: (_result, _error, { id }) => [{ type: 'Board', id }, 'Board'],
    }),
    deleteBoard: builder.mutation<void, string>({
      query: (id) => ({
        url: `/boards/${id}`,
        method: 'DELETE',
      }),
      invalidatesTags: ['Board'],
    }),
    // ===== LISTS =====
    getListById: builder.query<List, string>({
      query: (id) => `/lists/${id}`,
      transformResponse: (response: ApiResponse<List>) => response.data!,
      providesTags: (_result, _error, id) => [{ type: 'List', id }],
    }),
    createList: builder.mutation<List, { boardId: string; listData: CreateListDto }>({
      query: ({ boardId, listData }) => ({
        url: `/boards/${boardId}/lists`,
        method: 'POST',
        body: listData,
      }),
      transformResponse: (response: ApiResponse<List>) => response.data!,
      invalidatesTags: (_result, _error, { boardId }) => [
        { type: 'Board', id: boardId },
        'Board',
      ],
    }),
    updateList: builder.mutation<List, { id: string; updates: UpdateListDto }>({
      query: ({ id, updates }) => ({
        url: `/lists/${id}`,
        method: 'PUT',
        body: updates,
      }),
      transformResponse: (response: ApiResponse<List>) => response.data!,
      invalidatesTags: (result, _error, { id }) => [
        { type: 'List', id },
        { type: 'Board', id: result?.boardId },
        'Board',
      ],
    }),
    deleteList: builder.mutation<void, { id: string; boardId: string }>({
      query: ({ id }) => ({
        url: `/lists/${id}`,
        method: 'DELETE',
      }),
      invalidatesTags: (_result, _error, { boardId }) => [
        { type: 'Board', id: boardId },
        'Board',
      ],
    }),
    moveList: builder.mutation<List, { id: string; updates: MoveListDto, boardId: string }>({
      query: ({ id, updates }) => ({
        url: `/lists/${id}/move`,
        method: 'PUT',
        body: updates,
      }),
      async onQueryStarted({ id, updates, boardId }, { dispatch, queryFulfilled }) {
        const patchResult = dispatch(
          api.util.updateQueryData('getBoardById', boardId, (draft) => {
            const list = draft.lists.find(l => l.id === id);
            if (list) {
              list.position = updates.position;
              draft.lists.sort((a, b) => a.position - b.position);
            }
          })
        );
        try {
          await queryFulfilled;
        } catch {
          patchResult.undo();
        }
      },
      invalidatesTags: (_result, _error, { boardId }) => [{ type: 'Board', id: boardId }],
    }),
    // ===== CARDS =====
    getCardById: builder.query<Card, string>({
      query: (id) => `/cards/${id}`,
      transformResponse: (response: ApiResponse<Card>) => response.data!,
      providesTags: (_result, _error, id) => [{ type: 'Card', id }],
    }),
    createCard: builder.mutation<Card, { listId: string; cardData: CreateCardDto; boardId: string }>({
      query: ({ listId, cardData }) => ({
        url: `/lists/${listId}/cards`,
        method: 'POST',
        body: cardData,
      }),
      transformResponse: (response: ApiResponse<Card>) => response.data!,
      invalidatesTags: (_result, _error, { boardId }) => [{ type: 'Board', id: boardId }],
    }),
    updateCard: builder.mutation<Card, { id: string; updates: UpdateCardDto; boardId: string }>({
      query: ({ id, updates }) => ({
        url: `/cards/${id}`,
        method: 'PUT',
        body: updates,
      }),
      transformResponse: (response: ApiResponse<Card>) => response.data!,
      invalidatesTags: (_result, _error, { id, boardId }) => [
        { type: 'Card', id },
        { type: 'Board', id: boardId },
      ],
    }),
    deleteCard: builder.mutation<void, { id: string; boardId: string }>({
        query: ({ id }) => ({
            url: `/cards/${id}`,
            method: 'DELETE',
        }),
        invalidatesTags: (_result, _error, { boardId }) => [{ type: 'Board', id: boardId }],
    }),
    moveCard: builder.mutation<Card, { id: string; updates: MoveCardDto, boardId: string }>({
      query: ({ id, updates }) => ({
        url: `/cards/${id}/move`,
        method: 'PUT',
        body: updates,
      }),
      async onQueryStarted({ id, updates, boardId }, { dispatch, queryFulfilled }) {
        const patchResult = dispatch(
          api.util.updateQueryData('getBoardById', boardId, (draft) => {
            let cardToMove: (Card & { listId: string }) | undefined;
            let sourceList: (List & { cards: Card[] }) | undefined;
            // Find card and its source list
            for (const list of draft.lists) {
              const card = list.cards.find(c => c.id === id);
              if (card) {
                cardToMove = { ...card, listId: list.id };
                sourceList = list;
                break;
              }
            }
            if (cardToMove && sourceList) {
              // Remove from old list
              sourceList.cards = sourceList.cards.filter(c => c.id !== id);
              
              // Add to new list
              const destinationList = draft.lists.find(l => l.id === updates.listId);
              if (destinationList) {
                const movedCard = { ...cardToMove, listId: updates.listId, position: updates.position };
                destinationList.cards.push(movedCard);
                destinationList.cards.sort((a, b) => a.position - b.position);
              }
            }
          })
        );
        try {
          await queryFulfilled;
        } catch {
          patchResult.undo();
        }
      },
      invalidatesTags: (_result, _error, { boardId }) => [{ type: 'Board', id: boardId }],
    }),
  }),
});
export const {
  // Board hooks
  useGetBoardsQuery,
  useGetBoardByIdQuery,
  useCreateBoardMutation,
  useUpdateBoardMutation,
  useDeleteBoardMutation,
  
  // List hooks
  useGetListByIdQuery,
  useCreateListMutation,
  useUpdateListMutation,
  useDeleteListMutation,
  useMoveListMutation,
  
  // Card hooks
  useGetCardByIdQuery,
  useCreateCardMutation,
  useUpdateCardMutation,
  useDeleteCardMutation,
  useMoveCardMutation,
} = api;

`Error: @prisma/client did not initialize yet. Please run "prisma generate" and try to import it again.`

This means that the `associate-boards.ts` script is trying to import and use the Prisma Client, but the client code itself hasn't been generated in your `` directory. The `prisma generate` command is what reads your `schema.prisma` file and creates the tailored database client code.

_**Agent**_

Yes, that is correct. It's a good question, and the distinction is important for understanding how Prisma works.

### What `prisma generate` does

The `prisma generate` command reads your `schema.prisma` file and creates or updates the Prisma Client library in your `` directory. This client is a type-safe query builder tailored specifically to your database schema. When you added the `User` model, `prisma generate` is what makes `prisma.user` available in your code and makes TypeScript aware of it.

### Why it's needed in the script

1.  **Standalone Scripts vs. Development Server**:
    *   When you run `prisma migrate dev`, it automatically runs `prisma generate` for you after the migration succeeds.
    *   When you are running your backend server with `npm run dev:backend`, some setups might watch for changes and regenerate, but it's not guaranteed.
    *   The `associate-boards.ts` script is a **standalone script** run with `tsx`. It has no awareness of whether the schema has changed since the last time `prisma generate` was run.

2.  **Ensuring Consistency**: By adding `npx prisma generate` to the `script:associate-boards` command, we guarantee that the Prisma Client is perfectly in sync with the `schema.prisma` file right before the script attempts to use it. This prevents errors where the script tries to access a model or field (like `userId`) that the *code* knows about but the *generated client* doesn't yet.

In short, you are correct that Prisma has been working. Adding `prisma generate` to that specific script is a best practice to make it robust and prevent sync issues, especially in a project where the schema is evolving.

// scripts/associate-boards.ts
import { PrismaClient } from '../src/shared/generated/prisma';
const prisma = new PrismaClient();
const TARGET_USER_ID = '8ZWIzPZiEPbW4xlsIJFGawyHc7b2';
async function main() {
  console.log(`Associating unassigned boards with user ID: ${TARGET_USER_ID}`);
  // First, ensure the user exists in the database.
  // The auth middleware should have created this user on first login,
  // but it's good practice to check.
  let user = await prisma.user.findUnique({
    where: { id: TARGET_USER_ID },
  });
  if (!user) {
    console.log(`User with ID ${TARGET_USER_ID} not found. Creating...`);
    user = await prisma.user.create({
      data: {
        id: TARGET_USER_ID,
        // You might want to fill this in manually or leave as placeholder

  }
  // Find all boards that do not have a userId
  const unassignedBoards = await prisma.board.findMany({
    where: {
      userId: null,
    },
  });
  if (unassignedBoards.length === 0) {
    console.log('No unassigned boards found. Nothing to do.');
    return;
  }
  console.log(`Found ${unassignedBoards.length} unassigned boards. Updating...`);
  // Update the boards with the new user ID

    where: {
      userId: null,
    },
    data: {
      userId: TARGET_USER_ID,

  console.log(`Successfully updated ${updateResult.count} boards.`);
}
main()
  .catch((e) => {
    console.error('An error occurred while associating boards:', e);
    process.exit(1);
  })
  .finally(async () => {
    await prisma.$disconnect();
  });

}

The `@@map("boards")` directive tells Prisma that the  model corresponds to a SQL table named `boards`. Your script was trying to query a table literally named "Board", which doesn't exist.

This is a classic JavaScript modules error. The log `TypeError: admin.auth is not a function` is the key.

It's happening because of how the `firebase-admin` package is being imported in .

The current code has:
`import * as admin from 'firebase-admin';`

This syntax (`import * as ...`) bundles all exports into a single object named . However, the `firebase-admin` package is likely structured to be used with a default import when working with ES modules (which your backend is).

The fix is to change the import statement to a default import:
`import admin from 'firebase-admin';`

This will correctly import the `firebase-admin` SDK object, which has the `.auth()` method, and the `TypeError` will be resolved.

I have applied this change to . Please restart your backend server for the change to take effect.```typescript
import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import admin from 'firebase-admin';
import { AppError } from './errorHandler.js';
import { prisma } from '../services/database.js';
// Extend Request type to include user
declare global {
  namespace Express {
    interface Request {
      user?: admin.auth.DecodedIdToken & { id: string }; // Ensure id is available
    }
  }
}
/**
 * Middleware to verify Firebase ID token and handle user creation.
 */
export const authMiddleware = async (
  req: Request,
  _res: Response,
  next: NextFunction,
): Promise<void> => {
  // In test environment, mock user from a special header
  if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'test') {
    const testUserUid = req.headers['x-test-user-uid'] as string;
    if (testUserUid) {
      // This mock allows us to test authenticated routes
      req.user = {
        uid: testUserUid,
        email: `${testUserUid}@example.com`,
        name: 'Test User',
        id: testUserUid, // For consistency
      } as unknown as admin.auth.DecodedIdToken & { id: string };
      return next();
    }
    // If no header, proceed as unauthenticated to test protected routes
  }
  const authHeader = req.headers.authorization;
  if (!authHeader || !authHeader.startsWith('Bearer ')) {
    return next(new AppError('Unauthorized: No token provided or invalid format', 401, 'NO_TOKEN'));
  }
  const idToken = authHeader.split('Bearer ')[1];
  if (!idToken) {
    return next(new AppError('Unauthorized: Token is missing', 401, 'NO_TOKEN'));
  }
  try {
    const decodedToken = await admin.auth().verifyIdToken(idToken);
    // Check if user exists in our DB, if not, create them
    let user = await prisma.user.findUnique({
      where: { id: decodedToken.uid },
    });
    if (!user) {
      user = await prisma.user.create({
        data: {
          id: decodedToken.uid,
          email: decodedToken.email || '', // email is optional on firebase token
          name: decodedToken.name,
        },
      });
      console.log(`New user created: ${user.id} - ${user.email}`);
    }
    req.user = { ...decodedToken, id: user.id }; // Attach user to request
    next();
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error verifying Firebase ID token:', error);
    next(new AppError('Forbidden: Invalid or expired token', 403, 'INVALID_TOKEN'));
  }
};
```

This is an excellent catch! The error `TypeError: admin.auth is not a function` points to a subtle but critical mistake in the backend's authentication middleware.

The Firebase Admin SDK for Node.js requires you to call `admin.auth()` as a function to get the authentication service instance. The current code is likely trying to use it as a property (`admin.auth`), which is incorrect.

I will now correct this in `authMiddleware.ts` by changing the incorrect call to the proper function call. This will allow the middleware to correctly verify the Firebase ID token sent from the frontend, resolving the 403 Forbidden error. This is a classic `firebase-admin` SDK error, and it's due to an incorrect import statement for ES Modules.

The error `TypeError: admin.auth is not a function` happens because of this line in `authMiddleware.ts`:

```typescript
import * as admin from 'firebase-admin';
```

When using ES Modules (which your backend does), this `import * as ...` syntax imports the module's namespace, but not the `default` export where the main functionality lives. The `firebase-admin` package is designed to be used with a default import.

The fix is to change the import statement to correctly grab the default export.

I will now correct the import in `authMiddleware.ts`. This will align it with modern ES Module standards and resolve the `TypeError`.

_**Agent**_

This is another classic environment-specific error. The message `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND metadata.google.internal` is the key.

Here's what's happening:
1.  The backend code uses `admin.credential.applicationDefault()` to initialize the Firebase Admin SDK.
2.  This method is smart and tries multiple ways to find your credentials. One of its first attempts is to contact the Google Cloud metadata server at `metadata.google.internal`.
3.  This address only exists when your code is running inside a Google Cloud environment (like Google Cloud Run or App Engine). Since you're running on your local machine, the address can't be found, and the request fails.
4.  The SDK is failing to "determine project ID" because it can't reach that server.

The fix is to be more explicit in the initialization and provide the `projectId` directly, so the SDK doesn't have to guess. This will make it correctly use the `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` environment variable you've set, without trying to contact the metadata server.

I will update `server.ts` to include the `projectId` in the `initializeApp` call. Your project ID is `driftboard-backend`, which I can see from your frontend Firebase configuration.

I will now apply this fix.

_**User (2025-07-11 21:05Z)**_

Question, the variables are marked "Frontend Firebase Configuration" - but why would those values be on the frontend? Doesn't that expose things like ... the FIREBASE_API_KEY ?

---

_**Agent**_

That is an excellent and very important question. It's one of the most common points of confusion when working with Firebase, and it's smart to question it.

Here’s the breakdown:

### 1. Frontend API Key vs. Backend Service Account

You are dealing with two completely different types of credentials:

*   **Frontend API Key (Public):** The `VITE_FIREBASE_API_KEY` and other `VITE_` variables are for the **client-side SDK**. This key is **not a secret**. Its only purpose is to identify your specific Firebase project to Google's servers. It essentially says, "Hello, I am the DriftBoard web app." It does **not** grant any special permissions on its own. It's expected and required to be publicly visible in your frontend JavaScript code.

*   **Backend Service Account Key (Secret):** The credentials you have in `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` (the service account JSON file) are for the **Admin SDK**. This key is **highly sensitive and must be kept secret**. It grants full administrative privileges to your backend server, allowing it to bypass all security rules to act as an administrator (e.g., minting tokens, managing users). This is why it lives only on your server and is never exposed to the browser.

### 2. How is Firebase Secure Then?

Firebase security does not rely on hiding the frontend API key. It relies on two other powerful mechanisms:

1.  **Firebase Authentication:** This is what you've just set up. It ensures that a user is who they say they are. When a user logs in, they get a temporary ID Token. Every request to your backend API includes this token, and your `authMiddleware` verifies it. This proves the request is from a legitimate, logged-in user.

2.  **Security Rules (for Firestore/Storage):** If you were using Firestore or Firebase Storage directly, you would write Security Rules on the Firebase server. These rules define who can access what data. For example, a rule would say, `allow read, write: if request.auth.uid == resource.data.userId;`. This means "Only let a user access a document if their user ID matches the `userId` field on that document."

In your current architecture, your **Express backend acts as your security rules**. Your API endpoints check for a valid, authenticated user and then use Prisma to fetch only the data that belongs to that specific user.

**In summary: It is safe and correct to have the `VITE_` Firebase configuration on the frontend. The security of your application is enforced by your backend API, which validates the user's identity on every request.**

_**User (2025-07-11 21:33Z)**_

What is a "Redux slice", and how does it relate to auth state management?

---

_**Agent**_

Of course. A **Redux slice** is a core concept in [Redux Toolkit (RTK)](https://redux-toolkit.js.org/), which is the standard way to write Redux logic today.

Think of a slice as a **self-contained bundle of logic for a single feature or domain** within your application's state. Instead of scattering action creators, action types, and reducer logic across multiple files, a slice co-locates them into one file, making your code more organized and easier to maintain.

A slice automatically generates action creators and action types, which significantly reduces boilerplate code.

### How It Relates to Auth State Management in DriftBoard

For authentication, you would create an `authSlice`. This slice is responsible for managing all state related to the user's authentication status.

Here’s what the `authSlice` in your project (`authSlice.ts`) manages:

1.  **State Shape**: It defines the structure of the authentication state. This typically includes:
    *   `user`: The currently logged-in user's information (e.g., `uid`, `email`), or `null` if no one is logged in.
    *   `token`: The Firebase ID token (JWT) needed to authenticate with your backend API.
    *   `status`: A string to track the status of async operations like logging in (e.g., `'idle'`, `'loading'`, `'succeeded'`, `'failed'`).

2.  **Reducers**: These are pure functions that handle state changes. The `authSlice` has reducers for actions like:
    *   `setUser`: An action that runs when a user successfully logs in. It updates the state to store the `user` object and `token`.
    *   `logout`: An action that runs when a user logs out. It resets the state by clearing the `user` and `token`.
    *   `setLoading`: An action to set the `status` to `'loading'` while a login attempt is in progress.

3.  **Async Thunks**: For asynchronous operations like communicating with Firebase, the slice uses `createAsyncThunk`. For example, a `login` thunk would:
    *   Make an async call to Firebase to sign the user in.
    *   On success, it would dispatch the `setUser` action with the user's data.
    *   On failure, it would update the state with an error message.

In summary, the **`authSlice` is your application's single source of truth for "who is logged in."** Any component in your React application can access this state to:

*   Conditionally render UI (e.g., show a "Login" button or a "Logout" button).
*   Protect routes, ensuring only authenticated users can access certain pages.
*   Provide the authentication token to the RTK Query API so it can be sent with every request to your secure backend.

  "textEditContent": "# React Component Architecture in DriftBoard\n\nDriftBoard follows a structured and scalable component architecture designed to keep the codebase organized, maintainable, and easy to navigate. This document outlines the different types of components and their roles.\n\n## Core Principles\n\n- **Separation of Concerns**: Components are organized based on their function (UI, layout, pages, features).\n- **Composition over Inheritance**: We build complex UIs by composing smaller, single-purpose components.\n- **Reusability**: Common UI elements are abstracted into reusable components to ensure consistency and reduce duplication.\n\n## Component Directory Structure\n\nAll frontend components are located in &#96;/src/frontend/src/components/&#96;.\n\n### 1. UI Components (&#96;components/ui/&#96;)\n\n- **Purpose**: These are the foundational, \"dumb\" building blocks of our application's UI. They are highly reusable and have no knowledge of the application's business logic.\n- **Source**: Most of these components are from the **ShadCN/UI** library, which provides unstyled, accessible primitives.\n- **Examples**: &#96;Button.tsx&#96;, &#96;Card.tsx&#96;, &#96;Dialog.tsx&#96;, &#96;Input.tsx&#96;.\n- **Guidelines**:\n    - They should be styled with Tailwind CSS.\n    - They receive all data and callbacks via props.\n    - They should not contain any application-specific logic or fetch data.\n\n### 2. Kanban Components (&#96;components/kanban/&#96;)\n\n- **Purpose**: These are feature-specific components that are directly related to the Kanban board functionality. They often compose smaller UI components to build more complex features.\n- **Examples**: &#96;Board.tsx&#96;, &#96;List.tsx&#96;, &#96;Card.tsx&#96; (the Kanban card, not the UI primitive), &#96;BoardList.tsx&#96;.\n- **Guidelines**:\n    - These components might contain some business logic related to the Kanban feature.\n    - They interact with the Redux store to get data or dispatch actions.\n    - They are the core visual elements of the main application interface.\n\n### 3. Form Components (&#96;components/forms/&#96;)\n\n- **Purpose**: Reusable forms for creating and editing data, such as boards and cards.\n- **Examples**: &#96;BoardForm.tsx&#96;, &#96;CardForm.tsx&#96;.\n- **Guidelines**:\n    - They manage their own local form state (e.g., using &#96;useState&#96; or a library like &#96;react-hook-form&#96;).\n    - They receive an &#96;onSubmit&#96; callback from their parent component to handle the data submission.\n\n### 4. Layout Components (&#96;components/layout/&#96;)\n\n- **Purpose**: These components define the overall structure and layout of the application.\n- **Examples**: &#96;Header.tsx&#96;, &#96;Sidebar.tsx&#96;, &#96;AppLayout.tsx&#96;.\n- **Guidelines**:\n    - They often contain the main navigation elements.\n    - &#96;AppLayout.tsx&#96; typically wraps the page content, providing a consistent look and feel across the application.\n\n### 5. Page Components (&#96;pages/&#96;)\n\n- **Purpose**: Each file in this directory corresponds to a specific route or page in the application. They are the top-level components for a given view.\n- **Examples**: &#96;BoardsPage.tsx&#96;, &#96;BoardDetailPage.tsx&#96;, &#96;LoginPage.tsx&#96;.\n- **Guidelines**:\n    - They are responsible for fetching the initial data required for the page, usually via RTK Query hooks.\n    - They compose layout, kanban, and UI components to build the complete page.\n    - They connect the different parts of the application together.\n\n### 6. Higher-Order &amp; Special Components\n\n- **&#96;ProtectedRoute.tsx&#96;**: A component that wraps other components to restrict access to authenticated users only. It checks the auth state from the Redux store and redirects to the login page if the user is not logged in.\n",

  "isConfirmed": true,
  "content": "",
  "textEditContent": "# State Management in DriftBoard\n\nDriftBoard uses a layered approach to state management, leveraging both React's built-in hooks and Redux Toolkit (RTK) for a predictable, scalable, and efficient state architecture.\n\n## The State Management Hierarchy\n\nWe categorize state into four types and use the best tool for each job:\n\n1.  **Local/Component State**: Managed with &#96;useState&#96; and &#96;useReducer&#96;.\n2.  **Global UI State**: Managed with a dedicated Redux Toolkit slice (&#96;uiSlice&#96;).\n3.  **Server Cache State**: Managed with **RTK Query**.\n4.  **Global Auth State**: Managed with a dedicated Redux Toolkit slice (&#96;authSlice&#96;).\n\n---\n\n### 1. Local/Component State (&#96;useState&#96;, &#96;useReducer&#96;)\n\n- **When to Use**: For state that is only needed by a single component or a small, co-located group of components.\n- **Examples**:\n    - Toggling the visibility of a dropdown menu.\n    - Managing the input values of a form before submission.\n    - Tracking whether a dialog is open or closed.\n- **Why**: It's the simplest and most performant solution for local state. It avoids unnecessary re-renders of the entire application when only a small part of the UI needs to change.\n\n### 2. Global UI State (&#96;uiSlice&#96;)\n\n- **When to Use**: For global UI state that needs to be shared across different, non-related parts of the component tree.\n- **Examples**:\n    - Managing the state of a global notification or toast message system.\n    - Toggling a global sidebar or modal that can be triggered from anywhere.\n- **Why**: A Redux slice provides a centralized place to manage this state, making it accessible from any component without \"prop drilling\" (passing props down through many layers).\n\n### 3. Server Cache State (RTK Query)\n\n- **What it is**: This is not just data; it's a **cache** of the data that lives on your backend server. RTK Query handles the entire lifecycle of fetching, caching, and updating this data.\n- **When to Use**: For any data that comes from your API. This includes boards, lists, and cards.\n- **Why**: RTK Query is the most powerful tool in our state management arsenal. It automatically handles:\n    - **Fetching and Caching**: It fetches data and keeps it in the Redux store. Subsequent requests for the same data are served from the cache instantly.\n    - **Automatic Re-fetching**: It intelligently re-fetches data when it might be stale (e.g., when the user re-focuses the browser window).\n    - **Loading and Error States**: It provides simple hooks (&#96;useGetBoardsQuery&#96;) that return &#96;data&#96;, &#96;isLoading&#96;, &#96;isError&#96;, etc., which simplifies UI code immensely.\n    - **Mutations and Cache Invalidation**: When you update data (e.g., create a new board), you can \"invalidate\" the cached list of boards, which triggers an automatic re-fetch to keep the UI in sync.\n    - **Optimistic Updates**: For a super-responsive UI, you can update the local cache *before* the API call completes, and roll it back if the call fails. This is perfect for features like drag-and-drop.\n\n### 4. Global Auth State (&#96;authSlice&#96;)\n\n- **What it is**: A specialized Redux slice that holds the user's authentication status, user information, and JWT token.\n- **When to Use**: For managing the application's current user session.\n- **Why**: This state is fundamentally global. Many parts of the application need to know if a user is logged in:\n    - **&#96;ProtectedRoute&#96;**: To allow or deny access to pages.\n    - **&#96;Header&#96;**: To show a \"Login\" or \"Logout\" button.\n    - **RTK Query**: To grab the auth token and send it with every API request.\n\nBy separating state concerns this way, we keep the application organized, reduce complexity, and leverage the best tool for each specific scenario.\n",
  "toolCallResult": null
}
```

  "textEditContent": "# Routing in DriftBoard\n\nDriftBoard uses **React Router** (&#96;react-router-dom&#96;), the standard library for handling navigation in React applications. It allows us to create a single-page application (SPA) with multiple views or \"pages\" that can be accessed via unique URLs, without requiring a full page reload from the server.\n\n## Core Concepts\n\n### 1. Router Setup (&#96;main.tsx&#96; and &#96;App.tsx&#96;)\n\n- **&#96;BrowserRouter&#96;**: In &#96;src/frontend/src/main.tsx&#96;, the entire &#96;App&#96; component is wrapped in &#96;&lt;BrowserRouter&gt;&#96;. This component uses the browser's History API to keep the UI in sync with the URL.\n- **&#96;Routes&#96; and &#96;Route&#96;**: In &#96;src/frontend/src/App.tsx&#96;, we define the application's routes.\n    - The &#96;&lt;Routes&gt;&#96; component is a container for all possible routes.\n    - Each &#96;&lt;Route&gt;&#96; component maps a URL &#96;path&#96; to a specific React &#96;element&#96; (a page component).\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;tsx\n// Example from App.tsx\nimport { Routes, Route } from 'react-router-dom';\nimport { LoginPage } from './pages/LoginPage';\nimport { BoardsPage } from './pages/BoardsPage';\nimport { BoardDetailPage } from './pages/BoardDetailPage';\nimport { ProtectedRoute } from './components/ProtectedRoute';\n\nfunction App() {\n  return (\n    &lt;Routes&gt;\n      &lt;Route path=\"/login\" element={&lt;LoginPage /&gt;} /&gt;\n      &lt;Route \n        path=\"/\" \n        element={\n          &lt;ProtectedRoute&gt;\n            &lt;BoardsPage /&gt;\n          &lt;/ProtectedRoute&gt;\n        } \n      /&gt;\n      &lt;Route \n        path=\"/board/:boardId\" \n        element={\n          &lt;ProtectedRoute&gt;\n            &lt;BoardDetailPage /&gt;\n          &lt;/ProtectedRoute&gt;\n        } \n      /&gt;\n    &lt;/Routes&gt;\n  );\n}\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### 2. Dynamic Routes and URL Parameters\n\nTo create pages for specific items, like a particular Kanban board, we use URL parameters.\n\n- **Syntax**: A colon (&#96;:&#96;) in the path indicates a parameter (e.g., &#96;/board/:boardId&#96;).\n- **Accessing Params**: The &#96;useParams&#96; hook from &#96;react-router-dom&#96; allows a component to access these parameters.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;tsx\n// Inside BoardDetailPage.tsx\nimport { useParams } from 'react-router-dom';\n\nexport const BoardDetailPage = () =&gt; {\n  const { boardId } = useParams(); // e.g., if URL is /board/123, boardId will be \"123\"\n  \n  // Now you can use boardId to fetch the specific board's data\n  const { data: board } = useGetBoardQuery(boardId);\n\n  // ...\n};\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### 3. Navigation\n\nWe use the &#96;&lt;Link&gt;&#96; component or the &#96;useNavigate&#96; hook to navigate between pages programmatically.\n\n- **&#96;&lt;Link&gt;&#96; Component**: Use this for standard navigation, like links in a header or sidebar. It renders an &#96;&lt;a&gt;&#96; tag but prevents the default browser navigation.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;tsx\nimport { Link } from 'react-router-dom';\n\n&lt;Link to={&#96;/board/${board.id}&#96;}&gt;View Board&lt;/Link&gt;\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n- **&#96;useNavigate&#96; Hook**: Use this for navigation that happens as the result of an action, like after a form submission.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;tsx\nimport { useNavigate } from 'react-router-dom';\n\nconst MyFormComponent = () =&gt; {\n  const navigate = useNavigate();\n\n  const handleFormSubmit = async (data) =&gt; {\n    const newBoard = await createBoard(data).unwrap();\n    navigate(&#96;/board/${newBoard.id}&#96;); // Redirect to the new board's page\n  };\n  \n  // ...\n};\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### 4. Protected Routes\n\nA critical feature for any application with authentication is restricting access to certain pages. In DriftBoard, we use a custom &#96;ProtectedRoute&#96; component.\n\n- **How it Works**:\n    1. The &#96;ProtectedRoute&#96; component wraps the page component that needs protection.\n    2. It uses a Redux selector (&#96;useSelector&#96;) to check the authentication status from the &#96;authSlice&#96;.\n    3. If the user is authenticated, it renders the &#96;children&#96; (the actual page).\n    4. If the user is not authenticated, it uses the &#96;&lt;Navigate&gt;&#96; component from React Router to redirect them to the &#96;/login&#96; page.\n",

}
